newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam wins Hanoi venue for annual donor talks. [CORRECTED 12:56 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Vietnam wins Hanoi venue for annual donor talks. [CORRECTED 12:56 GMT]

text.p: Vietnam will hold its annual meeting with the donor community in Hanoi instead of Paris this year so that it can explain a new five-year economic plan, a senior World Bank official said on Friday.

The bank's resident representative in Vietnam, Bradley Babson, told Reuters that the Communist country would present its drive for "industrialisation and modernisation" at a Consultative Group meeting in Hanoi on December 5-6.
Consultative Group meetings, donor gatherings chaired by the bank, are usually held in Paris.
In a report ratified at the Communist Party's landmark congress two months ago, the government set a target of average economic growth of 9-10 percent a year between now and 2000.
The manifesto pledged to continue with reforms of the centrally planned economy, which have brought vigorous growth of more than eight percent annually since 1992.
The donor community has been increasingly sympathetic to Hanoi since the reform process and a more open-door foreign policy were adopted in the late 1980s.
At last year's Consultative Group meeting, donor nations and agencies praised the economic reform drive and performance and pledged to give $2.31 billion in aid.
A World Bank (Corrects from IMF) official said Hanoi had indicated it was looking for quality assistance rather than quantity this year because it was being more selective about development projects.

"So from that point of view, I would not expect the general level of funding to go up very significantly," he said. "...from their side, they would not be unduly upset if there was even a slight decline."
During the past three years, the donor community has pledged $6.5 billion to Vietnam, of which about $1.2 billion has come from the World Bank.
The World Bank, the main agency for channelling funds to developing nations, has proposed disbursing a further $500 million in soft loans each year between 1997 and 1999.

However, the rate of aid absorption has been slow. The World Bank has paid out about $180 million and the donor community as a whole has disbursed about $120 million, $250 million and $650 million in the three years from 1994 to 1996.

Separately, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a statement on Friday that it would consider an updated economic programme for Vietnam in November, opening the way for $88 million in soft loans to be granted under a structural adjustment deal.
The IMF approved the three-year, six-tranche enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) of about $525 million for Vietnam in 1994.
ESAFs are funds loaned by the IMF at concessional rates to low-income countries in return for a pledge to undertake strong policy steps, usually aimed at redressing balance of payments problems.

The IMF noted that Vietnam's export-led expansion was continuing and that despite continued rapid economic growth of around nine percent, inflation had fallen to about three percent from almost 20 percent a year ago.
